title: Leaving home
hookLine: in Allah's name, I trust in Allah, no power except by Allah (Abu Dawud; Tirmidhi)
tomorrow: a mosque has two doors in words. what's through each one?

cards: Keys, wallet, phone: the pat-down at the door, all three pockets. Then the step outside, where the checklist runs out.
The Prophet ﷺ gave a line for that step: bismillah, tawakkaltu 'ala Allah, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah. In Allah's name; I trust in Allah; there is no power and no strength except by Allah.
In Abu Dawud's telling, whoever says it is told: you are guided, you are sufficed, you are protected. And it carries an old question. If you trust God at the door, how much should you have packed?

teach.b: One view says: pack everything, then trust. When the Qur'an tells the Prophet to consult people and decide, it says, in Pickthall's words, "And when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah."
Resolve first; trust after. And Sahih al-Bukhari tells of people from Yemen who set out on pilgrimage with no provisions, saying, we are the ones who trust.
A verse came down: take provisions.
On this view, trust doesn't replace the checklist. It's what you say when the checklist is done. The other view says: you can never pack enough, and the line knows it.

No power and no strength except by Allah. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi says that if people trusted God as they truly should, they'd be provided for as the birds are: out hungry in the morning, home full at night.

On this view, the line's work is to let go, at the door, of what you can't carry: the worry riding along in the back seat. Each side has a best case. The planner's: the birds still fly out; no food lands in the nest.
The truster's: every bag ever packed still left something out. And the line itself holds both. It isn't said sitting on the couch.
It's said walking out. In Allah's name, the step.
I trust him, the letting go.

how: Muslims say this line, in Arabic, as they step out of the house; some families teach it to children as the thing to say at the door.

o: words said before a long fast, asking for strength
words said on coming home, greeting the family
words said at the door: in God's name, I trust Him

games.q: two views at the door — tap the pairs.
p: no power or strength but by Allah

s: in this tradition, trusting God means you shouldn't plan
the Qur'an says resolve, then trust; the Yemen travelers were told to take provisions.
the door line comes with a promise: guided, sufficed, protected
in Abu Dawud's telling, that's what's said to the one who says it.
in the birds hadith, the birds stay in the nest and food arrives
they go out hungry in the morning and come home full.

games.q: your aunt skips checking the weather before a road trip: 'i trust God.' your cousin calls that careless. give your aunt's best case.
o: no forecast covers everything; trust lets go of what you can't control.
checking the weather is a sign of weak faith, so it's actually wrong.
weather apps are always wrong anyway, so there's no point.
games.why: that's the truster's steelman. the planner answers with the Yemen travelers in al-Bukhari: take provisions. the line is said walking out, so it carries both.

practice: If you can, stand at a doorway, any door, with your hand on the handle or the frame. Feel the weight of whatever you're carrying today, in your bag and in your head.
Say the line once, or its meaning, and on the last words loosen your grip, without letting go.

wordCard.voice: Leaving home: the line for the doorstep. In Allah's name; I trust in Allah; no power and no strength except by Allah.

orig.note: Arabic: I have put my trust in Allah.

carryVoice: Your line: I trust him. Packed, and still trusting, one step past the checklist. Out the door.

sources.ref: Sunan Abu Dawud 5095; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3426 (the line for leaving home)
